quotes.quote: we introduce PolyMath, a multilingual mathematical reasoning benchmark covering 18 languages and 4 easy-to-hard difficulty levels
even Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking and Gemini-2.5-pro, achieve only 54.6 and 52.2 benchmark scores, with about 40% accuracy under the highest level

Current popular multilingual mathematical datasets, such as MGSM (Shi et al., 2023) and XSVAMP (Chen et al., 2024a), are too simple to evaluate the reasoning capabilities of advanced LLMs effectively.
most advanced and challenging benchmarks are available only in English
Therefore, creating a challenging multilingual mathematical reasoning benchmark is crucial for studying multilingual reasoning abilities in the current era of LLMs.
To bridge this gap, we build PolyMath, a multilingual benchmark organized by comprehensive difficulty levels, spanning from K-12 to Olympiad and advanced frontier mathematics.
PolyMath consists of 500 high-quality mathematical reasoning problems, with 125 problems at each level.
All original problems are presented in English and later translated into other languages
Our data collection process integrates two methods: incorporating existing publicly available benchmarks and scraping official repositories from the internet.
we directly source all 125 samples from MGSM (Shi et al., 2023) with 10 language versions
we select 25 problems from the HLE dataset (Phan et al., 2025), which represent challenging problems as perceived by the world’s top mathematicians
we assign problem levels entirely through human judgment by individuals with strong mathematical expertise, with each tag confirmed by two additional experts
our annotation pipeline consists of three stages: (1) LLM Pre-Translation: we first prompt GPT-4o to generate preliminary translations of the original English problem Q1 into various target languages
Experts extract about 30 terms per hour
Answers in our PolyMath are presented in diverse forms, including Numeric, Expression, Equation, Interval, Set, Tuple
Total Data 125*4*18=9000
By default, we set w1 = 1, leading to w2 = 2, w3 = 4, w4 = 8
solving eight low-level problems is equivalent to solving a single top-level problem in terms of contribution to the final score
K-12 Mathematics: Basic algebra, geometry, and probability & statistics, primarily presented as Math Word Problems (MWP).
Competitions (Top Olympiad): The highest-tier international/national/regional mathematics Olympiads, representing the upper limits of human IQ.
Total: 6,079 (∼75% of total world population)
Note: Please put the final answer in $\boxed{}$.
We set the maximum output token limit to 65,536
At each level, we obtain an accuracy (ACC) result for each model and language, corresponding to the pass@1 metric
For non-reasoning LLMs, we use greedy decoding for open-source models.
we use a hyperparameter setting of T = 0.6, p = 0.95, and k = 20 for open-source models
Each model is tested 16 times under fixed hyperparameters
we employ a rule-based matching script that achieves over 98% precision based on sampled human inspection
At the higher three levels, range typically stays around 10%, with some reasoning models, such as Qwen-QwQ-32B, reaching nearly 20%
fluctuations in multiple runs are mostly within 0.5–1.5% ACC
reasoning LLMs like Gemini-2.5-pro and Qwen-3-235B-A22B-Thinking still achieve nearly 40% ACC
Beyond performance, language consistency (LC) between input and output is also crucial, especially for users who only understand their native language.
we identify the language(s) of each output a for input q using the langdetect library
Non-Reasoning LLMs exhibit near-perfect LC across all levels
Reasoning LLMs consistently exhibit lower LC scores.
